title: Behavioral intention of gen Z towards society 6.0 in Nepal: An extension of UTAUT using PLS-SEM and ANN
content:
by Majibur Rahman Siddique, Niranjan Devkota, Purnima Lawaju, Dhan Bahadur Lowar, Udaya Raj Paudel, Ramkrishna Chapagain, Govinda Raj Upadhyay, Rheet Rijal

Society is inherently dynamic and has continuously evolved from Society 1.0 to Society 6.0. As an emerging paradigm, Society 6.0 extends the technology-oriented vision of Society 5.0 by integrating technological advancement with ethical governance, ecological sustainability, and inclusive well-being. Nepal, one of the fastest urbanizing countries in South Asia, faces increasing pressure to align with such evolving societal models. In this context, this study examines the behavioral intention of Gen Z toward Society 6.0 in Nepal. Grounded in a post-positivist philosophy, the study adopts a cross-sectional research design. Primary data were collected from 1,039 Gen Z respondents across all seven provinces using a stratified random sampling technique. The study employs a hybrid analytical approach combining PLS-SEM and ANN, using SmartPLS 4.1 and SPSS 29.0. The Unified Theory of Acceptance and Use of Technology (UTAUT) model was extended by incorporating societal trust as an additional construct, thereby offering a novel contribution that captures the role of trust as a critical determinant in the adoption of Society 6.0. The PLS-SEM results reveal that performance expectancy (β = 0.345, p < 0.001), societal trust (β = 0.239, p < 0.001), social influence (β = 0.176, p < 0.001), and facilitating conditions (β = 0.160, p < 0.001) significantly influence behavioral intention, while effort expectancy shows no significant direct effect. Mediation analysis indicates that performance expectancy mediates the relationship between effort expectancy and behavioral intention, and societal trust mediates the relationship between social influence and behavioral intention. The model explains 61.6% of the variance in behavioral intention (R2 = 0.616). The ANN findings further confirm performance expectancy as the most influential predictor, followed by societal trust, facilitating conditions, and social influence. The study offers practical guidance for policymakers to strengthen trust-driven governance and for educators to redesign digital curricula, alongside valuable insights for technology developers and civil society organizations advancing Society 6.0 in Nepal and the world.
